items.title: Ψάχνετε για Garba Near You This Navratri; Αυτός ο μηχανικός έφτιαξε έναν δωρεάν χάρτη με εκδηλώσεις σε 35 πόλεις
items.titleOriginal: Looking for Garba Near You This Navratri? This Engineer Built a Free Map of Events Across 35 Cities
items.description: Κάθε Navratri, ο Rajesh Hadiya, ένας 30χρονος μηχανικός λογισμικού στο Pune, βρήκε τον εαυτό του να κάνει την ίδια ερώτηση: πού είναι τα garbas κοντά μου; Ο λάτρης της γκουτζαράτι γκαρμπά δεν βρήκε ποτέ εύκολα την απάντηση και η αναζήτηση τον απογοήτευε χρόνο με τον χρόνο. Αυτόν τον Οκτώβριο αποφάσισε να σταματήσει την αναζήτηση και να αρχίσει να χτίζει. Στις 10 Οκτωβρίου 2026, το βράδυ πριν από το Navr…
items.descriptionOriginal: Every Navratri, Rajesh Hadiya, a 30-year-old software engineer in Pune, found himself asking the same question: where are the garbas near me? The Gujarati garba lover never found the answer easily, and the search frustrated him year after year. This October, he decided to stop searching and start building. On 10 October, 2026, the night before Navratri began, he put a free website online that places garba and dandiya nights across India on a single map. From a yearly frustration to a two-day build Hadiya has more than eight years of experience with Android and mobile apps and runs a developer community called DroidTribe. He reasoned that a problem this familiar could not belong to him alone. "If I have this problem, many others must have it too," he told DeshGujarat. He built the first version of Nearby Navratri in two days with Claude, an AI tool, and has added garbas and features every day since. The project runs on free tools and Cloudflare's free hosting, which leaves the domain name as his main expense. He told Mumbai Mirror that it has cost him only a few hundred rupees. Why a festival of nine nights needs a map Gujarat Tourism calls Navratri in the state a nine-night dance festival, perhaps the longest in the world. Garba, the circle dance at its heart, joined UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in December 2023 as the 15th element from India. UNESCO describes garba as a devotional dance for Shakti, the feminine energy worshipped during Navratri. Dandiya adds colourful sticks, and Nearby Navratri lists both kinds of night. Nearby Navratri brings garba and dandiya events across 35 Indian cities onto a single free map, helping people find venues, timings, entry fees and booking links. Photograph: ( Nearbynavratri ) With so many nights on offer, finding the right one takes effort. Some nights sell passes on third party platforms, while free society temple garbas often sell nothing online, according to the site. How the map works The site opens in a phone browser, with no app to download and no login, and its map runs on OpenStreetMap data. A visitor can tap "Show garbas near me" to see the closest nights first, with distances and directions, and the site says it never stores their location. Each listing gives the venue, dates, timings, starting pass price, and a link to the organiser's page for booking. Passes start at Rs 49, and filters narrow the map to free entry or to passes under Rs 500 or Rs 1,000. Many listings name the nearest metro station, and another filter hides nights whose listings say no stag entry. Readers can explore the map at nearbynavratri.in . The map spans 35 cities, from Ahmedabad, Surat and Vadodara to Mumbai, Pune, Bengaluru, Delhi NCR and Chennai, and it reaches smaller centres such as Bhuj, Navsari and Vapi. Room for the smaller garbas Hadiya said smaller events are a priority as he keeps expanding the map. Free neighbourhood and society nights, such as the Vokla Faliya Garbi in Old Bhuj and the Busa Society Sheri Garba in Bharuch, sit beside ticketed AC dome nights in Ahmedabad. From ticketed dance nights to free neighbourhood celebrations, Nearby Navratri lists events of different sizes, making it easier for people to discover garbas beyond the big venues. In the Mumbai region alone, Mumbai Mirror counted 43 events, including the free GM Navratri Mahotsav in Mira Road and a free garba night at VIBGYOR High in Belapur. Organisers and visitors can add an event for free, including society nights that sell no tickets online, by sharing a ticket or Instagram link and the venue's map pin. The site says it usually reviews each submission within a few hours. One person behind the listings Hadiya runs the site alone . He checks each submission against organisers' published prices and timings, accepts society garbas only if they admit the public and updates changes himself, according to Mumbai Mirror. The site collects listings from public event pages and organiser submissions. It says it has no affiliation with any organiser or ticketing platform and asks visitors to confirm details before they travel, because dates and prices can change. It also says it refreshes listings through the festival and removes events that end or are cancelled. What the response shows By 14 October, four days after launch, the site had 9,114 users, Mumbai Mirror reported. Hadiya said almost half of the Google searches that bring people to it ask for nearby dandiya nights, and about a third of visitors click through to a booking page. Navratri closes on Monday, 19 October, with Dussehra on 20 October. Mumbai Mirror reports that, if things go as planned, the map will return every year, so a festival built on knowing where to go may soon have a guide for every season. Sources ' App maps garba nights around you ': by AA Correspondent for Mumbai Mirror, Published on 14 October, 2026 ' Weekend Navratri Plans? items.descriptionOriginal: Το αίσθημα ότι μπορούμε να επηρεάσουμε την καθημερινότητά μας φαίνεται να έχει ιδιαίτερη σημασία για την ευτυχία όσο μεγαλώνουμε. Νέα μελέτη συνδέει την αίσθηση ελέγχου με μικρότερη συναισθηματική επιβάρυνση από τις αλλαγές που αποδίδουμε στην ηλικία. Την έρευνα, που δημοσιεύθηκε στο Psychology and Aging , παρουσιάζει η αναλύτρια συμπεριφοράς, Δρ. Wendy L. Patrick στο Psychology Today . Τι έδειξαν οι καθημερινές καταγραφές Στη μελέτη συμμετείχαν 268 ενήλικες ηλικίας 50 έως 91 ετών , οι οποίοι κρατούσαν ημερολόγιο για 14 ημέρες. Κατέγραφαν τις αλλαγές που αντιλαμβάνονταν ως απώλειες ή οφέλη της ηλικίας, πόσο ευτυχισμένοι αισθάνονταν και σε ποιον βαθμό θεωρούσαν ότι μπορούσαν να επηρεάσουν τη ζωή τους. Τις ημέρες που αναγνώριζαν περισσότερες απώλειες ή λιγότερα οφέλη από το πέρασμα του χρόνου, ανέφεραν χαμηλότερα επίπεδα ευτυχίας . Η σύνδεση αυτή ήταν εντονότερη όταν ένιωθαν ότι είχαν μικρότερο έλεγχο στην καθημερινότητά τους. Τι σημαίνει να αισθανόμαστε ότι έχουμε επιλογές Η αίσθηση ελέγχου αφορά την πεποίθηση ότι οι πράξεις και οι αποφάσεις μας μπορούν να επηρεάσουν όσα συμβαίνουν στη ζωή μας. Όπως εξηγεί η Δρ. Patrick, αυτή η αντίληψη μπορεί να κινητοποιεί την ενεργή αντιμετώπιση των δυσκολιών και την προσαρμογή στις αλλαγές της ηλικίας. Στο άρθρο της αναδεικνύει και έναν πιθανό φαύλο κύκλο: ο φόβος ενός τραυματισμού μπορεί να οδηγήσει σε περιορισμό της σωματικής δραστηριότητας , στερώντας ευκαιρίες διατήρησης της φυσικής κατάστασης. Αντίστοιχα, η απομάκρυνση από ευχάριστες ασχολίες μπορεί να περιορίσει τις πηγές καθημερινής ικανοποίησης. Χώρος και για όσα κερδίζουμε μεγαλώνοντας Η Δρ. Patrick στρέφει την προσοχή και στις θετικές πλευρές της ηλικίας , όπως η εμπειρία, η υπομονή και η μεγαλύτερη εκτίμηση των σχέσεων. Η αναγνώρισή τους μπορεί να διευρύνει την εικόνα που έχουμε για τον εαυτό μας πέρα από τις δυσκολίες και τους περιορισμούς. Οι ερευνητές προτείνουν να εξεταστεί η ενίσχυση της αίσθησης ελέγχου , μαζί με μια θετικότερη αντίληψη για τη γήρανση, στον σχεδιασμό παρεμβάσεων υποστήριξης των μεγαλύτερων ενηλίκων. Παρόλο που τα ευρήματα καταγράφουν συσχετίσεις σε διάστημα δύο εβδομάδων, χωρίς να αποδεικνύουν σχέση αιτίας και αποτελέσματος, αναδεικνύουν τη σημασία του να αισθάνεται κανείς ότι εξακολουθεί να έχει λόγο στις επιλογές της ζωής του. Διαβάστε επίσης 9 πράγματα που κάνει διαφορετικά ο «πιο ευτυχισμένος άνθρωπος στον κόσμο» – Δείτε βίντεο 5 τρόποι να βρούμε την ευτυχία μετά τα 50, σύμφωνα με μια ψυχολόγο Ευτυχία: Ποιο είναι το μυστικό του ευ ζην; Οι Ιάπωνες ξέρουν την απάντηση

items.descriptionOriginal: Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimer’s-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. The strongest benefits appeared at 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps, suggesting that the popular 10,000-step goal may not be necessary.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Soil Carbon Sponge Opens a New Path to Cooling the Planet Reading Time: 3 minutes A new report argues that restoring the soil carbon sponge could help cool the planet by rebuilding a hydrological system that has regulated heat for billions of years. The soil carbon sponge, Earth’s living water-management layer, may be one of the most overlooked tools in the fight against climate change. A new report argues that restoring healthy soil could help cool the planet directly. The idea centers on how living soil manages water, not just carbon. Researchers behind the report work with the Conscious Planet Save Soil initiative. Their analysis builds on decades of earlier work by Australian soil scientist Walter Jehne. The report frames water, not carbon alone, as the planet’s primary heat regulator. Water has shaped Earth’s temperature for roughly four billion years. Evaporation and condensation move enormous amounts of heat through the atmosphere. Healthy soil acts like a sponge that keeps this cooling cycle running. Underground fungal networks help build this sponge-like structure over time. Fungi bind soil particles together, creating tiny air pockets that trap water. That structure lets soil absorb heavy rainfall instead of letting it run off the surface. Right now, that sponge is badly damaged across much of the world. About 52 percent of global agricultural land is now considered degraded in some way. In parts of the United States, soil erosion runs up to ten times faster than natural formation. In Europe, an estimated 60-70% of soils are now considered unhealthy. Degraded soil holds less water and supports less plant growth. That shift pushes more solar energy into heating the air instead of evaporating water. Scientists describe this shift using two related terms: latent heat and sensible heat. Latent heat describes energy used to evaporate water, which cools the surrounding air. Sensible heat instead raises air temperature directly, as happens over dry, degraded land. Rebuilding soil organic matter could reverse much of this damage over time. The report estimates that each 1% increase lets a hectare hold 250,000 more liters of water. That stored water supports the plant growth needed for continued evapotranspiration. The report’s authors calculate that healthy evapotranspiration moves about 80 watts of energy per square meter. They compare this to the roughly 0.9 watts per square meter driving current global warming. Restoring the soil carbon sponge, they argue, could offset that imbalance several times over. This calculation reflects a newer and less mainstream approach within climate science. Most researchers still treat cutting greenhouse gas emissions as the primary lever for limiting warming. Even so, many scientists agree that healthy soil provides real, measurable local cooling benefits. Restoring the soil carbon sponge and cutting emissions are not competing strategies but complementary ones, with the report’s authors arguing that land regeneration and decarbonization pursued together can reinforce each other’s benefits across the same climate system. Photo by Sven Hornburg on Unsplash. The report’s authors frame soil restoration as a complement to emissions cuts, not a replacement. Both strategies address different parts of the same climate system. Pursued together, they argue, land regeneration and decarbonization could reinforce each other’s benefits. The report recommends several practical steps for restoring the soil carbon sponge. Cover cropping and mulching can keep bare soil from radiating heat back into the sky. Protecting forests also helps sustain the smaller, regional water cycles that keep landscapes moist. Researchers call these regional patterns small water cycles, distinct from the planet’s larger water cycle. Forests recycle much of their own rainfall internally, moistening the air around them. Losing forest cover can dry out a whole region even without any change in total rainfall. Some cities are already testing these ideas at a smaller scale. A trial in Canberra, Australia, is rewetting soil beneath open grassland to cool nearby streets. Early results suggest that even modest soil restoration can measurably lower local air temperatures. These recommendations echo growing interest in regenerative farming worldwide. Similar cover-cropping and mulching methods are already common practice for many small-scale farmers. Wider adoption could extend these local benefits across much larger areas. None of these steps require waiting on new technology to scale up. Farmers, land managers, and city planners around the world already have the tools to start today. Restoring the soil carbon sponge , one field at a time, could offer valuable climate protection. The post The Soil Carbon Sponge Opens a New Path to Cooling the Planet appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: I n August, videos of bulldozers ripping up the mouth of the iconic Santa Elena Canyon in Texas’ Big Bend went viral, propelling one of the country’s most remote national parks into the national spotlight. Construction crews were hard at work in the early stages of cutting a brand-new “patrol road” for law enforcement just feet away from an existing road to the canyon, whose 1,500-foot limestone cliffs, locals argue, form a natural border wall constructed millions of years ahead of schedule. Locals sprang into action, taking shifts monitoring construction and volunteering to rescue endangered plants — including the Chisos Mountain hedgehog cactus and all the spiny plants that provide protective nests for species like the yellow-billed cuckoo — ahead of the bulldozers. A rally was held on the beach in the shadow of the canyon, where people from all walks of life joined hands in the mud. “People think the Rio Grande divides us, but what the river actually does is unite us,” Hillary Pierce, an organizer with No Big Bend Wall, said into the bullhorn while holding a sign that said DON’T BULLDOZE MY CHURCH . The post A Wall Meant to Divide Is Uniting Left and Right in Texas appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Klamath River Salmon Comeback Surprises Scientists After Record Dam Removal Reading Time: 3 minutes Tribal advocacy and coordinated science monitoring made the Klamath River salmon comeback possible after a century of blocked rivers. The Klamath River salmon comeback is happening faster than scientists predicted. Chinook salmon have already reclaimed 88% of their historic territory in the upper Klamath River Basin. This progress comes just two years after crews finished removing four hydroelectric dams. A peer-reviewed assessment published in Scientific Reports offers the first quantitative look at how quickly migratory fish can recolonize a river system once barriers come down, and it treats the Klamath as a benchmark for restoration projects worldwide. The dam removal project wrapped up in October 2024. It stands as the largest dam removal effort completed anywhere in the world. Four dams, some over a century old, once blocked salmon from swimming upstream along the Oregon-California border. Researchers tracked the Klamath River salmon comeback using underwater sonar cameras positioned near the former dam sites. In 2024, about 7,700 Chinook salmon swam past the old dam locations. By 2025, that number grew to more than 13,000 fish, and together these salmon made up close to one-fifth of all Chinook returning to the entire Klamath Basin. Think of it like reopening a highway that had been closed for 100 years. Drivers did not just trickle back in. They found the route almost immediately and started using it in growing numbers. The salmon pushed through difficult terrain to get there. They swam through rocky whitewater stretches, climbed fish ladders taller than a two-story building, and crossed a 25,000-acre lake. One fish reached an elevation of 1,250 meters, more than 580 kilometers from the ocean, marking the farthest inland any Klamath salmon has been recorded and underscoring just how far this recovery has traveled. Scientists compared this recovery to other major dam removal projects. The Elwha River in Washington State saw a similar rebound after its dams came down. But the Klamath River salmon comeback reclaimed a larger share of old habitat in less time than any other large-scale project studied so far. Researchers believe geography helped speed things along. The upper Klamath Basin has broad, lake-filled headwaters instead of steep, narrow streams. This creates gentler terrain that suits salmon better than the sharp mountain drops found in many other river systems. The Klamath River salmon comeback is being aided by the basin’s own geography, with broad, lake-filled headwaters creating gentler terrain that suits returning salmon far better than the steep, narrow streams found in most other restored river systems. Photo by Gary Halvorson, Oregon State Archives on Wikimedia Commons . Cold, spring-fed rivers in the newly opened areas also help. These waters stay at steady, cool temperatures year-round. That gives salmon reliable conditions no matter the season or how much rain or snow falls that year. For over a century, four dams cut off salmon from these waters. Combined with overfishing and water withdrawals, the population had dropped by more than 90%. In 2002, roughly a quarter of that year’s entire salmon run died from disease tied to poor water conditions below the dams, a disaster that helped galvanize the movement behind today’s Klamath River salmon comeback. Removing the barriers has already reversed some of that damage. Beyond Chinook, researchers spotted coho salmon, steelhead, and Pacific lamprey exploring the reopened sections of the river. Their numbers remain smaller, but their presence shows the recovery reaches beyond a single species. Tribal nations played a central role in making this possible. The Yurok, Karuk, Klamath, and Shasta Indian Nation communities have relied on Klamath salmon for food, ceremonies, and cultural traditions for generations. Their decades of advocacy helped drive the push to remove the dams and set the Klamath River salmon comeback in motion. Scientists caution that early success does not guarantee lasting recovery. Most Klamath Chinook salmon live two to four years, so researchers need several more seasons before they fully understand how this generation will fare. They also want to see whether salmon start reproducing successfully in the newly reopened streams. One especially hopeful sign involves spring-run Chinook salmon, a variety that vanished from the upper basin decades ago. The newly reconnected cold-water streams could offer the right conditions for this ecotype to return, either naturally or through reintroduction efforts. Researchers plan to keep watching closely during the spring and summer months when these fish would typically appear. The momentum extends well beyond fish counts. River advocates have also pointed to broader gains, from clearer water to the return of native plants along the banks once buried under reservoirs, a shift that occurred as the dam removal project reached completion. What happens in the Klamath now offers guidance for river restoration projects worldwide. As more aging dams reach the end of their working lives, communities elsewhere face similar decisions. This basin shows that when rivers reopen, nature can respond with remarkable speed, and the Klamath River salmon comeback may just be the opening chapter of a much longer recovery story. The fish did not wait for permission. They found their way home. The post Klamath River Salmon Comeback Surprises Scientists After Record Dam Removal appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Αυτό που βρήκε ήταν μερικά κομμένα στο χέρι κοτσάνια του Γλυκού Γουίλιαμ, τα οποία φρόντισε μια Κρίστεν Φρίλαντ και οι κόρες της που δεν είχαν ιδέα για το τι ήταν αυτό…
items.descriptionOriginal: A grieving widower, still holding his loss from the day before, drove to a stranger's flower stand because his wife had asked to have her ashes scattered with wildflowers -- and he didn't know where else to look. What he found were a few hand-cut stems of Sweet William, tended by a Kristen Freeland and her daughters who had no idea what that ordinary summer afternoon meant to someone else. "What felt like an ordinary summer afternoon in our front yard was one of the hardest days of someone else's life," Freeland observed. A few simple blooms offered freely, without expectation or knowledge of its destination, became part of a sacred goodbye.

items.descriptionOriginal: When the paddy fields begin to ripen in Assam's Sonitpur district, two elephant herds start making a familiar journey. For much of the year, Tara and Phul, the female elephants leading these herds, remain in and around Sonai Rupai Wildlife Sanctuary. But as harvest season approaches, they move towards tea gardens, farmland and the islands of the Brahmaputra River. They often travel at night, passing close to homes, fields and roads. For a farmer, an elephant entering a field can mean losing a crop. For the animal, crossing a railway line or encountering frightened people can be dangerous, sometimes fatal. So how can we keep both safe when they need to share the same land? To find answers, the Assam Forest Department and WWF-India decided to follow the elephants themselves. Five elephants, 38000 locations. What did researchers find? Between April 2021 and June 2026, researchers fitted GPS collars to five elephants in Udalguri, Sonitpur and Biswanath, three Assam districts where encounters between people and elephants are a serious concern. Four were females travelling with their herds. The fifth was Bishu, a solitary, tuskless male in Biswanath. The collars recorded their locations over time, giving researchers more than 38,000 GPS locations across five years. Each location offered a small clue. Together, they showed which forests the elephants returned to, when they wandered towards farms and how they travelled between places that appeared disconnected on an ordinary map. The findings, published in October 2026 in a report titled Tracking the Giants , gave researchers a clearer picture of journeys that villagers often become aware of only when elephants appear near their homes. And one pattern stood out: the elephants travelled much farther during certain months of the year. The landscape also includes river corridors and other connecting habitats that animals use to move between feeding and resting areas. Photograph: (Saurav Borkatay/Roundglass Sustain) Why do elephants wander into farms every October? In Sonitpur, Tara and Phul's herds spent most of January to September within Sonai Rupai Wildlife Sanctuary. But between October and December, they ventured towards tea estates and settlements near Arimora Chapori, close to the Brahmaputra. Earlier observations by WWF-India also showed that these herds often crossed areas used by people at night, resting in tea gardens or forest patches during the day. A similar pattern emerged further west, in Udalguri. Here, two other female elephants, Mynow and Budhuni, travelled with their herds through Bornadi Wildlife Sanctuary, nearby reserve forests and tea plantations. Between October and January, their journeys extended into crop fields around tea estates such as Barangajuli, Dimakuchi and Paneri. The timing matters. These months overlap with the paddy season, when ripening crops can attract elephants towards farms. That brings them dangerously close to people trying to protect their harvests. But knowing when and where elephants are likely to appear could make a real difference. Instead of being caught unaware, forest teams and nearby communities could use these findings to prepare for their arrival and reduce the chances of dangerous encounters. What happens when an elephant's route crosses a border? The GPS collars revealed something else: the elephants' journeys rarely ended where a forest boundary did. Although Sonai Rupai, Bornadi and Behali wildlife sanctuaries were important habitats, the elephants also moved through tea estates, agricultural fields and river channels to reach other areas. Bishu, for example, travelled between Behali Wildlife Sanctuary and the Brahmaputra river islands that form part of Kaziranga National Park. Other elephants used river channels to move between forests along the Himalayan foothills and the grassy islands of the Brahmaputra, locally known as chaporis . For the elephants, these were routes connecting places they depended on. But some also passed through roads, railway lines and settlements, putting both animals and people at risk. And in Udalguri, researchers discovered that the elephants' journeys extended beyond India. During the dry season, the herds travelled into Bhutan's adjoining Jomotsangkha Wildlife Sanctuary. This discovery showed why keeping elephant routes safe requires cooperation between India and Bhutan, especially when the same herds move between both countries. Unlike isolated sightings, this long-term tracking provided a picture of how the animals used different habitats across seasons. Photograph: (Mongabay India) Could these GPS maps help save lives? The need for safer encounters is urgent. Between 2000 and 2023, elephant encounters claimed 1,468 human lives in Assam. During the same period, 626 elephants died from human-related causes, including electrocution, poisoning and railway collisions, according to figures cited in the study. The new GPS maps cannot prevent these tragedies on their own. But they can help forest officials understand where elephants regularly cross into areas used by people, identify dangerous stretches and plan ways to make these journeys safer. The report suggests measures around tea estates, including better lighting near settlements and roads, carefully planned fencing and discouraging crowds from approaching elephants. Researchers also observed how elephants responded to an existing conflict-management measure. In 2025–26, the Sonitpur herds did not enter Arimora Chapori after their movement along Sonai Rupai's southern boundary was blocked. Whether this change will make their journeys safer in the long run still needs to be studied. As Aritra Kshettry, who leads WWF-India's Elephant Conservation Programme, explains, understanding where elephants travel and how their movements change with the seasons can help authorities plan better ways to reduce conflict. Five elephants cannot tell researchers everything about every herd in Assam. But following their journeys has revealed something valuable: where elephants and people are most likely to cross paths, and when. That knowledge could help a farmer prepare before elephants reach a field, while giving the animals safer ways to move between the forests they depend on. And perhaps that is what makes these 38,000 locations so important. Each one brings researchers closer to understanding how people and elephants can share the same landscape more safely. items.description: Στις 11 Οκτωβρίου 2026, κάτοικοι, φοιτητές, εθελοντές και πολιτικοί αξιωματούχοι συγκεντρώθηκαν στις όχθες της λίμνης Jakkur στη βόρεια Μπανγκαλόρ για την 75η έκδοση του #IamBengaluru – Εθελοντής για Πάρκα. Σύμφωνα με δημοσιεύματα των μέσων ενημέρωσης, η εκδήλωση, με την υποστήριξη της Multigen…
items.descriptionOriginal: On 11 October 2026, residents, students, volunteers and civic officials gathered along the banks of Jakkur Lake in north Bengaluru for the 75th edition of #IamBengaluru – Volunteer for Parks. The event turned a weekend morning into a collective effort to care for the city's shared spaces. According to media reports, the event, supported by Multigen, brought together families, environmental organisations and public representatives for a clean-up drive and activities focused on environmental awareness . Among those present were former IIIT-B director Professor Sadagopan and Bengaluru North City Corporation commissioner Pommala Sunil Kumar. Sadagopan urged residents to move beyond voicing complaints and take part in sustained efforts to improve their surroundings. Citizen participation can help nurture greener public spaces. It also raises an important question: how can communities contribute without civic authorities stepping back from their responsibilities? At Jakkur, a phone-in joins the clean-up The event also brought that question into the conversation. As Mirror Now reported on 12 October, Commissioner Sunil Kumar acknowledged the challenges civic bodies face in managing waste and public littering . He said infrastructure alone could not solve the problem without a change in public behaviour. He announced a Tuesday phone-in session on solid-waste management, in addition to the existing Friday sessions. He also invited residents to monitor waste-management micro-plans at local mustering centres, where sanitation workers organise their work. The event also included de-weeding, plogging and workshops for children. Students from Greenfield Public School in Sampigehalli were among the participants. When a morning walk becomes a watering round At Vengaiah Lake in east Bengaluru, residents are using their daily walks to keep young trees alive instead of organising a large clean-up. In a report published on 15 May, Bangalore Mirror documented the Bhagiratha initiative. Lake walkers bring water in bottles and cans to nourish hundreds of saplings during the summer. Among them are K N Guruprasad, a resident of T C Palya, and Naveen A B. View this post on Instagram A post shared by ಬೆಂಗಳೂರು ದಕ್ಷಿಣ ನಗರ ಪಾಲಿಕೆ (Bengaluru South City Corporation) (@bscc.gba) Guruprasad brought cans and arranged for a private water supplier. Naveen also joined the effort, bringing water and collecting wastewater from his home's reverse-osmosis purifier for the saplings. Volunteers also help keep the lake's surroundings free of garbage. The initiative is noteworthy because it builds on an existing habit. Residents do not have to set aside a separate day for conservation. They fold it into a routine they already follow. Forty residents, one road, three hours In January, the problem was not litter around a lake but dust accumulating along a road in east Bengaluru. According to The Times of India, around 30–40 residents of Balagere, Panathur and Varthur, many of them IT professionals, gathered on 17 January to clean a 100-metre stretch between Balagere T-Junction and Varthur police station. Using money raised through crowdfunding, they rented equipment and removed a tractor-load of silt in about three hours. Residents said mechanical sweeping machines were not deployed regularly, so roadside dust built up and was stirred up by passing traffic. They also raised concerns about respiratory problems, allergies, damaged roads and risks to commuters and schoolchildren. Reclaiming a footpath, one wall at a time In March, more than 70 volunteers from CGI India, including children, took part in a clean-up and beautification drive along Old Madras Road in Indiranagar, Bangalore Mirror reported on 10 March. The stretch between Halasuru Lake and SV Road Metro Station had accumulated garbage and posters, and broken footpath slabs made it less welcoming for pedestrians. Working with the Greater Bengaluru Authority and the citizen collective The Ugly Indians, volunteers removed rubbish, cleared posters and repainted walls. A similar partnership emerged in Basavanagudi in May. On 17 May, residents, college students, volunteers and civic workers spent more than four hours clearing waste from Mallikarjuna Temple Street in NR Colony. Deccan Herald reported on 27 May that the drive followed complaints about garbage heaps, foul smells and public urination along a stretch used by students, hospital visitors and temple-goers. Bengaluru still needs reliable waste collection, street sweeping, sewage treatment, action against illegal dumping and sustained maintenance of parks and lakes. Photograph: (thebetterindia) Members of the Basavanagudi Ward 154 Residents' Association, APS College and BMS College segregated the waste, while municipal sanitation staff and engineers helped remove it using tractors and auto-tippers. Organisers said they intend to extend similar drives to other parts of the ward. What 75 minutes can tell us On 12 September, students from Christ University's Bannerghatta campus joined the Indian Ploggers Army and Bengaluru South City Corporation for a clean-up around Madiwala Lake. The New Indian Express reported on 13 September that the 75-minute plogging drive collected 110 kg of plastic waste. It filled 15 sacks with bottles, milk packets, wrappers and straws from within a 100-metre radius of the lake. It was the Indian Ploggers Army's 1,032nd drive, led by its founder Nagaraj, popularly known as Plog Raja. The haul shows what a short, organised effort can achieve. It also shows how much plastic reaches the edges of a public water body in the first place. Care as part of civic life Across these initiatives, one thread runs through: people are making care for shared spaces part of ordinary civic life. A student picking up a wrapper, a walker watering a sapling and a resident reporting illegal dumping can all help build a culture in which public spaces are not treated as somebody else's problem. But volunteerism cannot replace public services. Bengaluru still needs reliable waste collection , street sweeping, sewage treatment, action against illegal dumping and sustained maintenance of parks and lakes. Civic bodies must remain accountable for delivering them. The value of these citizen-led efforts lies not in showing that residents can do the government's work. It lies in showing how communities can change everyday behaviour, bring neglected problems to attention and work with public agencies to protect the spaces everyone shares. Η dev…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM An Australian device that splits rooftop solar power across an entire apartment building just won the country’s top design honor. Melbourne-based Allume Energy took the 2026 Australian Good Design Award of the Year for its SolShare system , which its creators describe as a “traffic controller for solar.” The device also won the sustainability award at the same ceremony, held Friday at ICC Sydney, where more than 1,000 entries competed across 13 disciplines. Why apartment solar access matters Homeowners with their own rooftops have driven most of the residential solar boom , but apartment dwellers have largely been on the sidelines. Individual rooftop installations don’t work well in shared buildings: the costs multiply, the wiring gets messy, and you need a separate inverter for each unit. SolShare cuts through that. One rooftop system, one installation, and the device handles distribution to each apartment automatically. Dr. Brandon Gien, chair of Good Design Australia, called it “an amazing piece of technology” and a beautifully designed solution to a complex problem. “Millions of people live in apartments, and many have had limited access to the benefits of rooftop solar ,” he said. “SolShare is a clever Australian design innovation that addresses that problem in a practical way, and it is already delivering benefits at significant scale.” One of the world’s oldest design competitions The Australian Good Design Awards go back to 1958. Past recipients of the top prize include the Cochlear hearing implant (2000), Marc Newson’s economy class seats for the Qantas A380 (2009), the Flow Hive beehive design (2016), and filmmaker James Cameron’s Deepsea Challenger submersible (2012). SolShare now sits in that lineup. Other sustainability winners at the 2026 awards The night’s other awards pointed the same way. Finnish company FabPatch won the fashion and textiles discipline for a rub-on fabric repair system. No Wrap , an Australian-designed reusable pallet securing system, and Holy Carp , a plastic-free compostable alternative to the soy-sauce fish packets in sushi packaging, both won gold in their categories. A ceremonial gathering space at Melbourne’s City Square, designed in collaboration with Wurundjeri elders to make Woi-wurrung language visible and welcome visitors to Country, won for the built environment. Sydney Children’s Hospital’s wayfinding project replaced standard clinical signage with native animals and plants grouped into three local environments: wetlands, sand dunes, and sea cliffs. Gien said the awards are meant to recognize design that can “bring joy to our lives, but not at the expense of the environment.” A small white box on an apartment wall that gets whole buildings into the solar conversation, without requiring anyone to overhaul the roof, is a reasonable candidate for that. Μέσα σε λίγα λεπτά, η ΕΕ ανακοίνωσε ότι απελευθερώνει 4,2 δισεκατομμύρια ευρώ (περίπου 4,6 δισεκατομμύρια δολάρια) σε κεφάλαια που δεσμεύτηκαν λόγω του κράτους δικαίου.…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Hungary’s parliament voted last Tuesday to repeal the 2021 Child Protection Law that banned the portrayal or promotion of homosexuality and transgender identities in schools and media. Within minutes, the EU announced it was releasing €4.2 billion (approximately $4.6 billion) in funds frozen over rule-of-law violations, a connection Budapest had been counting on. From political weapon to political liability Orbán’s government pushed the 2021 law as a child protection measure, framing gay and transgender people as a threat to public morals, and for years it worked. Then his government pardoned the deputy head of a children’s home convicted of covering up his boss’s child sexual abuse crimes, and what had been a political asset became the defining scandal of his final term. Magyar ran his campaign on protecting children in state care and largely sidestepped the LGBTQ rights issue; his party needed conservative votes, and he was not going to risk alienating them. Five years of legislation, unwound in one vote Tuesday’s package went beyond the 2021 law, touching Fidesz-era changes to education policy and assembly rights. Civil rights group Háttér Society , which had been fighting the child protection law for five years, said most of the problems it had flagged in the draft had been fixed. “We are very happy that this got adopted,” said Tamás Dombos of Háttér Society. “We’ve been fighting this so-called child protection law for five years.” The repeal also cleared Hungary’s path to rejoin Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe , two major EU programs suspended during the Orbán years over rule-of-law violations. Tisza holds the same two-thirds parliamentary majority Orbán’s party once had, which meant the package passed without needing to negotiate. Beyond the repeal Háttér Society welcomed the vote, though the group was clear about how much remains unaddressed. It still wants full recognition of same-sex marriage , adoption rights for same-sex couples, and the right of transgender people to change their names on official documents, none of which are in the new legislation. Magyar has been careful in how he frames the issue. “I’m very cautious,” he told Finnish daily Helsingin Sanomat. “As prime minister, it’s my duty to represent all Hungarians, and we have sensitive issues, such as the situation of sexual minorities.” “We are still knocking on a closed door,” Dombos said, “but at least they are listening on the other side.” For a community that spent years being actively targeted, that is a real shift, even if full equality is still a long way off. Ενώ οι κραυγές της πόλης χρονολογούνται από την αρχαία Γρ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Hear ye, hear ye! You may not be aware, but town criers still exist — and the best of the bunch recently came together to show off their skills in an international competition. Held in Chester, England, the World Town Crier Tournament took place late last month with 25 competitors from eight nations. While town criers date as far back as ancient Greece and Rome, their prevalence in England beginning in the Middle Ages resulted in the image many associate with the role today. Literacy rates were much lower then, so criers were responsible for communicating news, beginning announcements with an exclamation of “oyez,” which is pronounced “oh yay” and derives from a French word meaning “to listen.” Decked out in period attire, the 2026 tournament participants performed three cries: one on their home towns, one on a retail store that sponsored the event, and another on their hotel accommodations. They were judged on vocal power, clarity, showmanship, and audience engagement. Kevin Howarth from Queensland, Australia, was named the overall winner, while Joris Goens of West Flanders, Belgium, took second place. Representing the host country, Christian Ashdown from Surrey, England, came in third. Ashdown spoke to SWNS after the event, describing his win as “a very pleasant surprise.” The 57-year-old noted that “there were some top criers” at the competition — and he would know. He’s been crier of Haslemere, a historic market town in Surrey, for 16 years and has won prior championships. A projects and amenities officer for the Haslemere Town Council, Ashdown said he never intended to be a town crier, but when his predecessor decided to retire in the middle of the busy Christmas period, the mayor called asking if he’d fill in. He hesitantly accepted and eventually fell in love with the role. He’s now the chair of the Ancient and Honourable Guild of Town Criers , which is the largest and oldest body of town criers in the world. Ashdown says there are 117 members and that town crying is becoming more popular as the guild has begun posting on social media. The job mostly consists of greeting people on special occasions and market days, as well as representing the town during contests. Criers must wear a costume, which is usually Georgian-inspired as that was the peak of town crying in England. Because they generally work on a volunteer basis, many hold down other jobs as well. “It had never crossed my mind to become a town crier. I knew what they were, but I didn’t know they still existed,” said Ashdown. “I knew nothing about it, but I have very much embraced it.” He added: “People love it and they thank me. It is all positive which surprised me actually.” Despite the perception of town criers being artifacts of the past, he noted that the position “has never really died off funnily enough. It is something that has never gone away.” He said that common mistakes are saying “oyez” while talking, rather than at the start of a cry with a pause, and focusing too much on volume. He also advises fellow or aspiring criers not to use their voice too much the day before an event, as they’ll need lots of water and throat lozenges. “Try not to scream and shout too much. You have to pace yourself,” Ashdown explained. “Just be nice and clear. It is not necessarily always about the volume; it is enunciation.” This article was originally written by Isobel Williams for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets. items.descriptionOriginal: Eating too much salt may do more than raise blood pressure. It could also harm memory and social behavior. In a new study, Japanese researchers discovered that a soy-derived compound called LPC70 helped protect mice from several damaging effects of a high-salt diet. Mice given the supplement had lower blood pressure, better memory, and improved social interactions compared with mice consuming excess salt alone.

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have uncovered three brain pathways linked to lasting improvements in people receiving deep brain stimulation for severe, treatment-resistant depression. They also discovered that patients who failed to improve after two years shared a striking pattern: insufficient stimulation of a crucial brain connection. The findings suggest that millimeters in electrode placement could make a major difference in treatment outcomes.

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have uncovered a surprising difference in how male and female skin repairs and renews itself. By tracking individual skin stem cells in living mice for five months, researchers discovered that female cells work together in a highly coordinated way, while male cells operate more independently. This synchronization, driven by sex hormones, helps explain why wounds heal faster in female mice, especially during the first few days.

items.descriptionOriginal: At 8,849 metres above sea level, there is little room for anything except the next step. On 21 May 2026, as Shradha Gupta stood on the summit of Mount Everest, the world below seemed to disappear. Around her stretched a landscape of snow, ice and distant ridgelines, while the summit itself offered barely enough space to stand. After years of balancing boardrooms, client calls and a demanding banking career with early-morning workouts and long weekends in the mountains, the 41-year-old banker from Delhi had finally reached the highest point on Earth. "I didn't know I was going to Kilimanjaro when I started hiking. When I started Kilimanjaro, I had no idea that I was going to be at Everest," she tells The Better India. Perhaps that is what makes her journey remarkable. Everest was not a childhood ambition mapped out over decades. Just three years before standing on its summit, Shradha had only recently rediscovered something she had loved as a child: mountains. Today, she has climbed five major summits across three continents, including four of the Seven Summits — Kilimanjaro in Africa, Elbrus in Europe and Aconcagua in South America — along with Manaslu and Everest in the Himalayas. But for Shradha, the story begins long before the summit photographs. It begins with a glass table, a long recovery, and a realisation that life had been passing by. The accident that made her look back Shradha has spent two decades in banking. Originally from Delhi, she left India at 17 to study engineering in Singapore and eventually joined DBS Bank, beginning her career on the trading floor. She spent 11 years in Singapore before moving to Dubai with the same bank in 2017. Today, she leads corporate business for the Middle East. For years, work had naturally occupied much of her life. Then, in 2020, an accident at home changed the way she looked at it. Shradha's first major expedition to Mount Kilimanjaro in 2023 helped her discover that she could take on climbs she had once thought impossible. A glass table caused a severe forehead injury that required reconstructive surgery. The bone had broken, muscles had torn, and her doctors had to piece everything together layer by layer. Her recovery took around 18 months. "The first one to two months was really bad. I couldn't even walk properly because it affected my balance, and it used to hurt all the time," she recalls. The experience left her thinking about how close she had come to losing the life she knew. It also made her wonder about everything she had postponed. "I think for me it ended up just being a life-changing experience," she adds. "I started thinking about how life had taken over, how work had taken over, and you just keep going year by year, and you forget about the things that are important to you and the ones that give you joy." One of those things had always been mountains . Growing up in Delhi, Shradha remembers her parents packing the family into their car during school holidays and heading towards the hills. Nainital, Mussoorie, Pithoragarh, Sangla Valley and other parts of Himachal Pradesh were part of her childhood. She had even climbed Mount Fuji with her parents as a teenager and later hiked in Malaysia while studying in Singapore. But a long gap passed before she returned to the mountains. That changed in February 2022. From weekend hikes to a much bigger dream A friend invited Shradha on a hike in Dubai with a group of women. Until then, she had associated Dubai with skyscrapers, not mountains. "I didn't even know that I could hike in Dubai," she says. "I had no idea that there were mountains like two hours away." After that first hike, she kept returning, heading almost every weekend towards the mountains around Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah. The hikes became her place to switch off, move and feel like herself again. Then came an old bucket-list dream: Mount Kilimanjaro. With her 40th birthday approaching, Shradha decided she did not want to keep waiting. "I don't know how long my body and mind are going to support me. So, if I have to do this, then let's just do it. There's no point waiting anymore." There was one practical problem. Kilimanjaro could take seven to nine days, and Shradha had never been unavailable for that long in her corporate career. She leads a business dealing with large corporate clients, so being disconnected was unfamiliar territory. From Kilimanjaro in Africa to Elbrus in Europe and Aconcagua in South America, each summit prepared Shradha for the challenges of Everest. Eventually, she found an expedition during the Eid break, giving her a week away from work. In June 2023, she set off. It was also her first expedition with strangers: five women, including three Indians, an Algerian and an Egyptian, along with one husband and their British expedition leader. The mountain gave them something in common. "You're there for each other, supporting, talking about your life stories, and sharing food together." More importantly, Kilimanjaro showed Shradha that she could actually do this. "I learnt that I could climb when I almost thought it was impossible," she shares. One summit kept leading to another After Kilimanjaro, Shradha travelled to Everest Base Camp in October 2023. It was there, while watching the sunrise from Kala Patthar, that the thought first appeared. She looked at Everest as the sunlight emerged behind it and thought, "One day, I want to stand on top of that mountain." It was not yet a plan, but the idea never took a back seat. Preparing for Everest meant balancing a demanding corporate career with hours of daily training. Her next test was Mount Elbrus, Europe's highest mountain, in June 2024. If Kilimanjaro had tested her at altitude and Everest Base Camp had tested her endurance over a longer journey, Elbrus introduced her to technical climbing on ice and snow. Then came Aconcagua in January 2025, the highest mountain in South America and the highest peak outside Asia. Each expedition, she says, became a way of introducing one new variable. Higher altitude. Longer duration. More technical terrain. By then, Everest was no longer just a thought. Before attempting it, though, Shradha wanted to test herself at 8,000 metres. In September 2025, she climbed Manaslu, the 8th-highest mountain in the world, at 8,163 metres, with Elite Exped. It was her first 8,000er and a completely different world from the mountains she had climbed before. There were fixed ropes, ladder crossings, crevasses, avalanches and the extreme conditions of what mountaineers call the "death zone". "Once you're in the 8,000-metre degree, it's a completely different world," she says. "It is harsh, and almost every day it's like you're fighting for your life because you don't know what's going to go wrong." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Shradha Gupta 🇮🇳 🇦🇪 🇸🇬 (@iamshradhagupta) Manaslu confirmed that she was ready to attempt Everest. But it also showed her exactly how much preparation would be required. Preparing for the mountain while holding down a career Training for Everest became another full-time commitment layered on top of her actual job. In Dubai, Shradha hikes whenever she can. During the summer, when temperatures can make outdoor training difficult, she uses Ski Dubai's indoor slope. Her routine also includes weightlifting, incline treadmill sessions, StairMaster workouts, swimming and running. At peak training, she was spending nearly two and a half to three hours exercising each day, split between mornings before work and evenings afterwards. Her Everest coach, Mike McCastle, based in Las Vegas, USA, began working with her in January 2026. Despite a shoulder injury, injured ribs and a persistent cough during her Everest expedition, Shradha continued towards the summit one step at a time. "She began fit. She finished expedition-ready," he says. McCastle's programme focused not just on cardiovascular fitness but on the demands of an expedition: loaded uphill movement, strength endurance, muscular durability, recovery and the ability to keep working after fatigue had accumulated. For him, Shradha's age was not the defining factor. "I coach the athlete standing in front of me, not the number written beside their age," he says. What stood out instead was her consistency . "She was balancing a demanding professional career, travel, stress and normal life alongside Everest preparation," McCastle says. "Consistency does not mean executing a perfect programme for months. It means continuing to return to the process when life disrupts the programme." Everest asked for everything she had The Everest expedition in 2026 did not go according to plan. With conflict in the Middle East creating uncertainty around air travel, Shradha left Dubai for Delhi in late March to complete her preparation without risking delays closer to the expedition. For Shradha, reaching Everest's summit meant pushing through one of the most physically demanding experiences of her mountaineering journey. On the mountain, she slipped on an ice wall in the Khumbu Icefall and injured her left shoulder, leaving her barely able to lift a one-litre bottle. With the route through Khumbu also delayed, she returned to Kathmandu for four days to recover before coming back to the mountain. Then came the dreaded Khumbu cough. The relentless dry cough left her sleep-deprived and progressively weaker. By the time she began her summit push, she was dealing with injured ribs, illness and exhaustion. "Nothing has tested me the way Everest has tested me," she says. "I have never been this hurt, this injured and this sick on a climb as I was on Everest." Still, she kept moving, drawing on a lesson she had learnt on Kilimanjaro: break the biggest goal into smaller steps. "My only responsibility today is to deal with today. We will deal with tomorrow when it comes." Shradha's first Kilimanjaro expedition brought together women from different backgrounds, united by the challenge of climbing Africa's highest peak. Her coach, Mike McCastle, saw the same resilience. "Mountains punish rigidity. Weather changes. Bodies change. Plans change," he says. "Shradha experienced setbacks during both training and the expedition... But she kept recalibrating." When she finally reached the summit, there was happiness and gratitude, but the climb was not over. She still had to descend, with an exhausted body and little left in the tank. She had to keep walking. There is still another mountain somewhere For Shradha's family, watching her journey from weekend hikes to 8,000-metre peaks has been its own experience. While the early expeditions worried them less, Manaslu and Everest were different. She stayed in touch with them through a satellite communicator, even as she remained aware of the risks. Before attempting the 8,000ers, she signed body-disposal forms, knowing that preparation cannot eliminate every danger. "When you're entering the world of 8,000ers, you are prepared to die," she says. "I know the risks that I'm going through. Sure, I will fight till my last breath to survive, but sometimes it may be out of my control." From weekend hikes to Everest's summit, Shradha's journey is a reminder that every big dream begins with one step. Today, she is back between Dubai and Delhi, returning to the corporate life she has continued alongside the mountains. But three years after that first hike, Everest is behind her, and the journey still feels far from over. For someone who once thought of mountains as family holiday destinations, there is perhaps no better way to look ahead than with the lesson that has carried her this far. "Whatever your dream is, it doesn't have to be mountains. It can be anything in life. Take that first step." She adds, "You may not be at your strongest. You may not be at your best. But if you want it bad enough, if you're giving it everything that you've got, the world will come together to make it happen for you." And so, after Everest, there is still another first step waiting somewhere ahead. All images courtsey of Shradha Gupta

items.descriptionOriginal: At 12:54 am on 7 March 2024, a small wild cat approached a man-made pond in a forest patch near Goa's Bhagwan Mahavir Wildlife Sanctuary. It stopped to drink, unaware that a camera trap beside the water was recording its movements. The camera captured five short video clips, which would soon become an exciting discovery for wildlife researchers Akshita Pungaliya and Atul Borker. The visitor was a mainland leopard cat ( Prionailurus bengalensis ), a shy, elusive wild cat that had never been photographically documented in Goa, according to the researchers' published findings. The sighting became the state's first reported photographic record of the species, with the findings published in the IUCN Species Survival Commission's Cat News in 2025. But the researchers hadn't set out looking for a leopard cat. Their project began with a much simpler concern. Every February, a freshwater stream running through this forest patch would dry up, leaving animals with fewer places to drink as the hotter months approached. Akshita and Atul wondered whether a small artificial pond could make water available to wildlife during those months. They decided to create one and use a camera trap to see what happened. What they recorded would help them understand the animals using this forest, including one that had rarely been documented in the region. When the forest ran out of water Akshita and Atul have long been interested in wildlife species that receive less attention than animals such as tigers and elephants. In 2023, the two researchers co-founded Vanasa Conservation Foundation to work towards protecting lesser-known wildlife. Their work brought them to a patch of private forest land bordering Bhagwan Mahavir Wildlife Sanctuary, where a seasonal stream offered an opportunity to understand how animals cope with disappearing water sources. "We wanted to understand if creating an artificial water source in these forest patches would actually be used by animals," Akshita tells The Better India. "We've been monitoring activity across the year, but the original plan was to provide it in the drier months." Before building the pond, however, the team wanted to find a spot that animals were already likely to visit. They walked through the forest looking for small trails, fruit remains and disturbed leaf litter. These were clues that mammals regularly passed through certain parts of the landscape. "We looked at places where we could see smaller trails made by mammals, food lying around, signs that told us this is a walking path they use," Akshita explains. Using these signs, they chose a suitable location, dug a small pond, lined it and filled it with water. The artificial pond had a capacity of 40 litres. A camera trap placed nearby would help the team find out whether animals discovered the water and, more importantly, whether they returned. As the recordings began coming in, the researchers got their first answers. The mainland leopard cat is one of Asia's most widespread wild cats, found across parts of India, Southeast Asia, China, Taiwan, Japan and the Russian Far East. Photograph: (Camera Trapped) Birds, squirrels and leopards began visiting The camera soon captured birds arriving to drink, mongooses stopping by and squirrels moving across the frame. As monitoring continued, the researchers began seeing larger visitors too, including Indian gaur and leopards. Giant squirrels also appeared in the footage. Some animals came so close to the camera that it could barely capture their bodies. Akshita recalls moments when "you can barely see the hooves." For a team hoping to understand whether wildlife would use the pond, the variety of visitors was encouraging. But what caught Akshita's attention was how some animals appeared to be returning to the same spot. "If we keep it on across seasons in the year, you see them getting used to that spot," she says. "Earlier they may have found it by chance, but now they recognise it." The repeated visits suggested that some animals were becoming familiar with the water source. Meanwhile, the camera was helping the researchers observe wildlife that might otherwise pass through the forest unseen. Across 390 camera-trap nights, they documented visits by several species. Among those recordings were the five clips of the mainland leopard cat drinking from the pond on 7 March 2024. "My co-founder and I were just really excited to see that this happened," Akshita says. Their excitement came from knowing how difficult it could be to photograph a species like this, particularly in a region with so few previous records. A wild cat that Goa had never photographed The mainland leopard cat is actually one of Asia's most widespread wild cats. It is found across parts of India, Southeast Asia, China, Taiwan, Japan and the Russian Far East, and is listed as Least Concern by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). Yet there are still gaps in our understanding of where these cats live in India. Most records come from the southern Western Ghats, the Himalayas and the Northeast. In the northern Western Ghats, photographic sightings have been particularly scarce, with only two previously documented in the wider region. Wildlife checklists had suggested that leopard cats could occur in Goa, but researchers lacked photographic evidence from the state. The footage from Akshita and Atul's pond helped fill that gap. Part of the challenge is the animal's behaviour. Leopard cats are small, shy, mostly active at night and often move through dense vegetation, making them difficult to observe. "This cat doesn't work the same way tigers or leopards do," Akshita explains. "It's small, elusive, shy, and mostly active at night." Researchers can sometimes recognise individual cats through their coat markings, but obtaining repeated camera-trap records across large forests takes considerable time and effort. And that effort needs funding, which can be difficult to secure for lesser-studied species. "Wildlife research highly depends on funding," Akshita says. "And funding often goes towards larger species or species in conflict with humans." As a result, smaller carnivores often receive less research attention, even though they perform important roles within forests. Leopard cats, for instance, feed on rodents and other small animals, helping regulate prey populations. Understanding their movements and habitats can help researchers learn more about how these forest ecosystems function. This is why even a single confirmed photographic record can be valuable. It tells scientists that a species is present in a particular landscape and gives them a starting point for further research. For Akshita, the Goa finding also shows what can emerge from a relatively small conservation experiment. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Nature's Nest Goa (@natures_nest_goa) Could more forests benefit from this idea? Creating an artificial pond like the one used in the project costs approximately Rs 30,000 to Rs 40,000, Akshita estimates. A basic camera trap can cost between Rs 8,000 and Rs 10,000, while a higher-end model costs around Rs 25,000. "This is in general a very low-cost plan," she says. The pond can provide a water source during dry months, while the camera trap helps reveal which animals visit the surrounding area. Akshita says nature resorts in Karnataka have already begun discussing similar interventions. For privately owned properties bordering forests, carefully planned projects like these could offer a way to contribute to conservation while learning more about local wildlife. But they also require an understanding of how different animals might respond. For instance, if smaller animals begin using the pond, could larger predators follow? "It could," Akshita says. "And I'm very sure a lot of bigger cats do use these areas, and maybe nature resorts don't even know them yet." That possibility makes careful monitoring important. People living or working near forests may have little idea of the different species passing through their surroundings, especially at night. And as Akshita points out, learning about those animals doesn't always require creating a new water source. "If you want to know what's in your backyard," she says, "sometimes you don't even need a waterhole. Just set up camera traps near good forest habitat." Her team's experience in Goa offers an example of why that curiosity matters. They began by noticing a stream that dried up every February. They followed the paths animals had made, created a small pond and placed a camera beside it to see who would come. The footage revealed a variety of animals visiting the water, including a leopard cat that had never been photographically documented in Goa before. Five short video clips gave researchers a new wildlife record and drew attention to a small wild cat that remains poorly studied in this part of India. And it all began because two researchers noticed that the animals in a patch of forest might need somewhere to drink.

items.descriptionOriginal: "1 Plant, 100 Uses" explores the many ways familiar Indian plants, leaves, fruits and trees have been part of everyday life — from food and farming to homes, traditions and natural remedies. Each story takes one plant and uncovers the surprising ways people have found it useful, often across generations. Sugarcane is a familiar sight across India's agricultural landscape. Its sweet juice is a popular summer drink; its stalks are crushed to make sugar and jaggery, and its leaves can be used as cattle fodder. But the plant's usefulness does not end when the juice has been extracted. India produced 454.61 million tonnes of sugarcane in 2024-25, according to the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare's Agricultural Statistics at a Glance 2024-25. Beyond sugar production, the crop also supplies raw materials for industries that use its fibrous residue and other by-products. From generating electricity and making paper to producing compostable tableware and enriching agricultural soil, sugarcane offers several uses beyond the kitchen. Even the fibrous residue left after crushing the stalks can become a valuable raw material for industries. Research by Indian agricultural institutions highlights how different parts of the crop can be put to use. Here are ways this everyday plant finds a purpose well beyond the sugar bowl. 1. Sweeten everyday foods Sugar is the most familiar product made from sugarcane. Its juice is processed to extract sucrose, then crystallised into the sugar used in homes, restaurants, and food manufacturing. Sugarcane is a familiar sight across India's agricultural landscape. Photograph: (Saveur) The crop also supplies traditional Indian sweeteners such as gur (jaggery) and khandsari sugar. Jaggery is made by boiling concentrated sugarcane juice until it solidifies and is widely used in regional sweets, laddoos, halwas, and traditional preparations. The Government of India's One District One Product portal provides further information on sugarcane-based products such as jaggery and molasses. 2. Make a refreshing drink Fresh sugarcane juice is a popular street-side drink across India, particularly during summer. Vendors crush the stalks to extract the juice, often serving it with lemon, ginger, or mint. The juice can also be boiled down to make jaggery. In traditional production, the fibrous residue left after extraction may be burnt to provide heat for boiling the juice. This allows one part of the plant to help process another. 3. Create compostable tableware The fibrous residue left after extracting sugarcane juice is called bagasse. Its fibres can be processed into plates and other disposable tableware, offering an alternative to conventional plastic products. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research's Central Institute for Research on Cotton Technology has developed a technology to produce disposable paper plates using sugarcane bagasse and banana pseudostem fibres. According to ICAR's technology note on creating wealth from agricultural waste , a production unit could manufacture between 10,000 and 30,000 paper plates a day, depending on its size. The process uses compression moulding to turn the fibres into usable products. This provides sugarcane-processing industries another way to use the residue left behind after crushing the stalks. 4. Generate electricity Bagasse can also serve as fuel. Sugar mills burn this fibrous residue in boilers to produce steam, which drives turbines to generate electricity. The electricity helps meet a mill's own energy requirements, while facilities with suitable infrastructure can supply surplus power to the grid. According to a Press Information Bureau release from the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy , sugar mills have used bagasse-based cogeneration plants to produce steam and electricity for their operations and generate additional power for sale. 5. Turn waste into paper Bagasse contains cellulose , a component of plant fibres used in paper manufacturing. After suitable processing, it can be converted into paper and other fibre-based products. The Institute of Wood Science and Technology, under the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education , explains how bagasse can be used to manufacture particle boards. It also identifies the material as a potential source of pulp for paper production. Its juice is processed to extract sucrose, then crystallised into the sugar used in homes, restaurants, and food manufacturing. Photograph: (Gardening Know How) Using this residue can create another source of raw material for industries that rely on plant fibres. 6. Feed farm animals Sugarcane can support livestock farming, too. The green tops and leaves left after harvesting can be used as dry fodder for cattle, particularly when conventional fodder is scarce. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research's study on sugarcane trash as fodder explains how the material can be chopped and mixed with green fodder and concentrate feed. Its nutritional limitations mean it should be used as part of a balanced ration rather than as a complete feed on its own. 7. Enrich agricultural soil Press mud, also known as filter cake, is a by-product separated during sugar juice clarification. It contains organic matter and plant nutrients that can be useful in agriculture. After appropriate treatment, it can be incorporated into compost and soil amendments, helping return organic matter to farmland . Its composition should be checked before application to make sure it is suitable for the intended use. This provides another route for putting sugar-industry residues to productive use instead of treating them solely as waste. 8. Make particle boards Sugarcane bagasse can be used to manufacture particle boards, which are made by processing plant fibres or particles and binding them into sheets. These boards can be used in certain furniture and interior applications. The Institute of Wood Science and Technology's research on bagasse particle boards describes the material's fibre content and its potential in board manufacturing. This application turns a residue from sugar production into a material that can serve the construction and furniture industries. Fresh sugarcane juice is a popular street-side drink across India. Photograph: (Juice at Home) One crop, many possibilities Sugarcane's value lies not just in its sweet juice but also in the many products that can be made from its different parts. Making better use of these materials can reduce waste and create additional value for sugar mills and farmers. The key is to choose suitable processing methods so that more of the crop can be used productively.

items.descriptionOriginal: Ten years after a childhood bike crash, Rika Matsuda unfolded an origami crane a stranger who witnessed the crash had given her and found a message written inside -- a Japanese expression meaning "cherish the moment," or more fully, that we should treasure each encounter because it may never come again. The man had slipped the words in quietly, without drawing attention to them, letting them wait until she was ready. What the story reveals is something almost too simple to name: that a caring stranger's gentleness, offered in a few unhurried minutes at a water fountain, can fold itself into a life and stay there. "He didn't say anything," Matsuda recalled. "He just smiled and handed me the origami crane."

items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine arriving at a popular tourist destination alone. You want to explore the place, take in the landscape, and spend a few hours at your own pace. But what happens if you feel unsafe, cannot find a working public facility, or need help navigating an unfamiliar area? And who do you turn to if something goes wrong? For women travelling alone, access to assistance can shape how comfortable they feel exploring a place. Kerala is seeking to address these concerns through its Green Marshal initiative, which aims to place trained personnel at selected tourist destinations to assist visitors, monitor safety and improve the upkeep of public spaces. The first phase is expected to create around 180 jobs, bringing local workers into the day-to-day management of tourist destinations. More than a safety checkpoint The Green Marshals are being envisaged as a visible, accessible point of contact for visitors. Their responsibilities will include monitoring tourist spots, assisting travellers, identifying problems and helping ensure that basic facilities remain functional. For a women exploring an unfamiliar destination, knowing whom to approach when she needs assistance can make a difference. The presence of trained personnel could also help visitors report concerns and seek support without having to navigate an unfamiliar administrative system. The initiative comes at a time when independent travel is an important part of the tourism landscape . Women travelling alone may have to assess unfamiliar surroundings, access to facilities and the availability of help while planning their journeys. However, the effectiveness of such a programme will depend on more than deploying personnel. Their visibility, training, ability to respond to complaints and coordination with the relevant authorities will determine how useful they are when a visitor actually needs help. The tourism department has indicated that Green Marshals will receive training in environmental responsibilities, destination management and interactions with tourists. This is intended to prepare them for the range of situations they may encounter while on duty. Who looks after the destination? Safety is only one part of the programme. Green Marshals will also be responsible for maintaining cleanliness, overseeing waste management and contributing to environmental protection at the sites where they are deployed. The tourism department has indicated that Green Marshals will receive training in environmental responsibilities, destination management and interactions with tourists. Photograph: (indiaunbound) A tourist destination is not simply a place people visit. It is also a public space that requires regular maintenance. Waste left behind by visitors, poorly maintained facilities and gaps in waste disposal can affect both the visitor experience and the surrounding landscape. Their role could be particularly relevant at destinations where visitor numbers place pressure on local infrastructure and natural surroundings Can local employment strengthen tourism? The first phase is expected to generate around 180 jobs. Beyond creating employment, the initiative proposes a role for local workers in managing the places that attract visitors to their communities. People familiar with a destination may be well placed to identify maintenance gaps, guide visitors and flag emerging concerns . Yet, the programme's long-term impact will depend on how it is implemented. The destinations selected for deployment, the number of personnel stationed at each site, the availability of reporting mechanisms and the process for responding to complaints will all matter. So will clarity on how Green Marshals coordinate with police, tourism officials and other relevant agencies when a situation requires intervention beyond their remit. When in Kerala, make time for Kovalam! #DreamSeason #InGodsOwnCountry #TravelVibes #KeralaTourism https://t.co/wKrSoYu40f — Kerala Tourism (@KeralaTourism) September 9, 2026 For women, the important question will ultimately be whether assistance is accessible and effective when needed. For the environment, it will be whether regular monitoring translates into better waste management and more responsible upkeep . A destination becomes more welcoming not merely when people arrive, but when they can explore it with confidence and when the place itself is cared for. Whether Green Marshals can deliver on that promise will become clearer as the programme takes shape across the state's tourist spots. Sources: 'Kerala To Deploy Green Marshals At Tourist Destinations From October' : By Rooplekha Das, Published on 14 September 2026 'What is Green Marshals, the Kerala initiative aimed at boosting women's safety?' : By Debolina Roy, Published on 14 September 2026
